stops.name: Genoa: the weaver's house, Vico Dritto di Ponticello
stops.campa: Between the feast of the Assumption and All Saints, a son is born to Domenico Colombo, wool-weaver and keeper of the Olivella gate, and to Susanna Fontanarossa. The house stands in the lane by the Porta Soprana; the looms clack below, and beyond the walls the harbor breathes. The boy is christened Cristoforo, Christ-bearer, and the name is a prophecy the whole canon will spend itself fulfilling. The family moves later to Savona, keeps a tavern, cards wool; the sea keeps calling through the shop door.
stops.quote: Being born in Genoa... from it I came and in it I was born.

stops.name: Chios: the mastic island of the Genoese
stops.campa: To sea young, as he later says: at fourteen. On Genoese ships he sails the length of the Middle Sea and comes to Chios, the mastic island the Mahona of Genoa holds against the Turk. He watches the lentisk trees bled for their fragrant tears, learns cargo and reckoning and the smell of the Levant trade. Eighteen years later, standing in Cuban forests, he will swear he knows mastic when he sees it; Chios is the proof he carries.
stops.quote: I have seen it in the island of Chios, in the Archipelago.
stops.quote_source: Diario of the first voyage, 12 November 1492 (Las Casas abstract)

stops.name: Off Cape St Vincent: the sea-fight and the burning ship
stops.campa: He sails as a hand in a Genoese convoy bound for England when, off the holy promontory of St Vincent, the corsair fleet of Guillaume de Casenove Coullon falls upon it. All day the ships grapple and burn, chained hull to hull; fireships and pitch. The vessel under him takes flame to the waterline. Men leap into a sea already full of the dead. Columbus, wounded, goes into the water six miles from land. The sea, which has drowned better swimmers for less, does not take him. It is keeping him for something.

stops.name: Lagos: ashore on an oar
stops.campa: An oar floats free of the wreck and he takes it, pushing it before him, swimming and resting, swimming and resting, six miles of open water with a wound in him, until his feet find the sand at Lagos in the Algarve. Fishermen carry him in; the town that fitted out Prince Henry's caravels nurses the half-drowned Genoese. When he can walk he goes to Lisbon, where his brother Bartholomew draws charts. The canon marks it plainly: the sea delivered him onto Portugal's doorstep, into the one school on earth that could teach him the Atlantic.

stops.name: Lisbon: the chart-maker's shop with Bartholomew
stops.campa: In Lisbon the brothers Colombo draw and sell sea-charts to the pilots of the most ocean-going city in Christendom. Every rutter and every rumor passes across their table: the Guinea coast, the new islands, the flotsam of unknown woods that the west wind throws onto Atlantic beaches, the two drowned men once cast up whose faces were of no known nation. Columbus learns Portuguese, Castilian, Latin, the art of the portolan. In the margins of his books, Ptolemy, Marco Polo, Pierre d'Ailly, the idea begins to take notes on itself.

stops.name: Ultima Thule: a hundred leagues beyond Iceland
stops.campa: In the dead of a northern February he sails on a Bristol trader past Galway, where he notes the strange-faced castaways men call Cathayans, and beyond, to the island the ancients named Thule. He records that the sea there was not frozen and the tides ran mightily. In the harbors of Iceland old men still tell of lands to the west, Greenland and beyond, where their grandfathers' ships once traded. The Admiral files the north away in silence. The Ocean has edges everywhere except where he intends to go.
stops.quote: In the month of February, 1477, I sailed a hundred leagues beyond the island of Tile... And to this island, which is as big as England, the English come with their wares, especially from Bristol.
stops.quote_source: Columbus's note, quoted in Ferdinand Columbus, Historie, ch. 4

stops.name: Lisbon: marriage at the Convento dos Santos
stops.campa: At Mass in the church of the Convento dos Santos, where the well-born boarders of the Order of Santiago hear the office, the Genoese chart-seller catches the eye of Dona Felipa Moniz Perestrelo, daughter of Bartolomeu Perestrello, first captain-donatary of Porto Santo. They marry. In one stroke the wool-weaver's son enters the small nobility of the Discoveries: his mother-in-law opens her dead husband's sea-chest and gives him the captain's papers, charts, and logs of the Atlantic islands. The dowry of the marriage is the Ocean itself.

stops.name: Porto Santo: the island of the dying pilot
stops.campa: He lives on Porto Santo, where his son Diego is born, and at Funchal in Madeira, shipping sugar for the Genoese houses. Here the Atlantic teaches him its private grammar: the northeast trades going out, the westerlies coming home, the strange canes and carved wood the sea lays at his door. And here the legend sets its scene: a storm-broken caravel, a dying pilot carried into Columbus's own house, who before death gives his host the bearing of a land seen far to the west, and the reckoning of the way back. The secret is buried with him; the bearing is not.

stops.name: Lisbon: Toscanelli's letter and chart
stops.campa: Through a Florentine of Lisbon he obtains the letter the physician Paolo dal Pozzo Toscanelli once wrote to the King of Portugal, with its sea-chart of the westward way: Antilia the island of the Seven Cities for a waystation, then Cipango roofed in gold, then Quinsay of the Great Khan, the whole Ocean shrunk to a crossing a brave fleet might make. Toscanelli writes to Columbus himself, praising his great and noble desire. The old cosmographer dies; the chart sails on. Columbus will carry a copy of it into the Ocean Sea.

stops.name: São Jorge da Mina: the Guinea voyage
stops.campa: He sails under the Portuguese flag to the Gold Coast, to the new fortress of São Jorge da Mina, where the gold of the Akan country comes down to the sea. He watches degrees of latitude fall away toward the equator and finds the burning zone of the ancients full of rain, trade, and living men: the schoolbooks are wrong about what is uninhabitable, and he is now a witness against them. He measures, he doubts the doctors, he trusts the deck under his feet. The Ocean's southern door is Portugal's; he begins to covet the western one.
stops.quote: I was at the fortress of La Mina of the King of Portugal, which lies below the equinoctial line, and so I am a good witness that it is not uninhabitable, as they say.
stops.quote_source: Letter to the Sovereigns on the Third Voyage, 1498

stops.name: Lisbon: King João II refuses the Enterprise
stops.campa: He lays the Enterprise of the Indies before João II, the Perfect Prince: the westward crossing, the titles, the tenth of all gains. The king's junta of cosmographers, men who know the true girth of the earth better than the petitioner, find his degrees too short and his words too large, and counsel refusal. The king, canny, is said to send a caravel secretly out on Columbus's own bearing; it comes back beaten by weather, having found nothing. Felipa dies. Debts gather. In the night, with little Diego on the saddle before him, Columbus slips out of Portugal for Spain.

stops.name: La Rábida: the friary on the Rio Tinto
stops.campa: A dusty foreigner leading a small boy knocks at the gate of the Franciscan house of Santa María de La Rábida, above the meeting of the Tinto and the Odiel, and asks bread and water for the child. The porter brings them; the guardian brings the friars. Fray Antonio de Marchena, who reads the stars, hears the stranger out. And believes him. It is the first belief the Enterprise has ever met. Diego is left in the friars' keeping like a pledge given to God, and letters go out from the friary toward the court of Castile.
